Sky, Moon and astronomy

On this page
  • Sun
  • Day & night
  • Moon
  • Eclipses
  • Sky: the planets
  • Geographic info: magnetism
  • The sky sphere

Besides prayer times, the Calendar screen has modes for the Sun, day and night, the Moon, eclipses, the planets and the Earth's magnetic field. Each mode follows the day selected in the month calendar. The home screen also has the Sky sphere, a 3-D view of the sky.

To change mode, tap the mode's name in the calendar's title bar, or step with the double arrows. See Calendar and Islamic occasions.

Sun

Day

The day's Day length first, then the nine events from dawn to dusk: Astronomical dawn, Nautical dawn, Civil dawn, Sunrise, Solar noon, Sunset, Civil dusk, Nautical dusk and Astronomical dusk, with the direction (azimuth) of sunrise and sunset. It also shows how long the Sun's disc takes to rise and to set (Sunrise takes, Sunset takes), and, under The Moon, the day's Moonrise and Moonset.

Far from the equator, an event that does not happen is named rather than given a time, for example "Above the horizon all day".

Chart

The Sun's altitude through the day, with the part below the horizon, the twilight bands, and the Sun's altitude and azimuth now. It is the same chart as in the prayer mode, without the prayer times.

Seasons

The year's equinoxes and solstices, each with its date, time, weekday and Hijri date, and the length of each season (Length:). A drawing shows the Earth's orbit seen from above, with the seasons. Under it: Sun's ecliptic longitude, Earth–Sun distance and Earth–Moon distance now. South of the equator, the season names are swapped.

Day & night

  • Times: the day from sunrise to sunset with its length, midpoint and the fasting length (Fasting (Fajr to Maghrib)); then the night in two ways, The night: sunset to Fajr and The night: sunset to sunrise, each with its length, midpoint and when Last third begins.
  • Dial: the whole day as a 24-hour ring, midnight at the bottom and noon at the top, coloured by Night, Astronomical twilight, Nautical twilight, Civil twilight and Daylight, with marks for sunrise, midday, sunset, midnight and the last third. The day and night lengths are in the centre. On today, a hand shows the time now.
  • Year: the length of the day, the Night to sunrise and the Night to Fajr through the year, with the selected day marked. Tap the chart to select a day.
  • Map: the world's daylight now (or at the selected day): day, twilights and night over a world map, with markers where the Sun and the Moon are overhead (Sun overhead at, Moon overhead at). Under it, a chart of the Sun's and the Moon's declination through the year.

In polar regions, a day without sunrise or sunset says "The Sun stays up all day" or "The Sun stays down all day", and a night without Fajr says "Dawn is not reached".

Moon

In Moon mode, the month calendar marks the days of the New moon, First quarter, Full moon, Last quarter, Perigee (closest to the Earth) and Apogee (farthest). Tap a marked day to see the event and its time.

Position

Where the Moon is now on the selected day: its azimuth, altitude, right ascension, declination, elongation, distance and constellation, and whether it is above or below the horizon. A diagram shows the Sun, the Earth and the Moon from above (Not to scale).

Phases

A picture of the Moon lit as it looks now, the phase name, the day's phase event and its time, the Illumination, the Moon's age since the new moon, the lunation number, moonrise and moonset, and the next main phase.

Distance

A chart of the Earth–Moon distance over the year, with every perigee (filled dot) and apogee (hollow dot) and a line at the selected day. Under it: Distance now, Apparent diameter, the next perigee and apogee, and the year's closest and farthest.

Crescent

This page predicts whether the new crescent can be seen after sunset on the selected evening. Two buttons at the top switch between At your place and All over the world.

At your place shows, for the selected evening:

  1. The title, such as "Crescent of Ramadan 1448 AH", the evening's date and the verdict in large type.
  2. Best time to look and the Conjunction (the astronomical new moon) nearest that sunset.
  3. Sunset and moonset, with their times and directions.
  4. The Moon at the best time: Moon age, Illumination, Moon azimuth, Moon altitude, Elongation, Crescent width, and the result of the two criteria, Odeh and Yallop.
  5. The month at a glance: the three evenings from the conjunction, one line each with its verdict. Tap a line to select that evening.
  6. First sighting by eye and First sighting with optical aid: the first evening each becomes possible.

All over the world shows the selected evening on a world map. Every area is coloured by its verdict, and lines join the places where the Moon has the same age at sunset, labelled in hours. Taqwim shows Computing… while it works. If the crescent cannot be seen anywhere yet, the map is replaced by a notice that names the first evening worth looking.

What the crescent verdicts mean

The verdict follows Odeh's criterion (2004), with Yallop's criterion (1997) shown beside it, both at the best time to look after sunset.

VerdictMeaning
The crescent can be seen with the naked eyeOdeh zone A: visible without help in a clear sky
The crescent can be seen with optical aid, maybe by the naked eyeOdeh zone B: binoculars or a telescope find it; the eye may then see it
The crescent can be seen with optical aid onlyOdeh zone C: only with binoculars or a telescope
The crescent cannot be seenOdeh zone D: not even with optical aid

Some evenings have no verdict, and the page says why:

  • Sunset comes before the conjunction: the new moon has not happened yet at sunset.
  • The Moon sets before the Sun: there is no crescent in the sky after sunset.
  • The Sun does not set this day, or No moonset near sunset: possible far from the equator.

Yallop's categories, shown under Yallop:

CategoryMeaning
AEasily visible
BVisible in perfect conditions
CMay need optical aid to find
DNeeds optical aid to find
ENot visible with a telescope
FNot visible, below the Danjon limit

On the world map, the colours are Naked eye, Optical aid, maybe by eye, Optical aid only, Not visible, Moon sets first and Sunset before conjunction.

These are predictions. "Real sightings depend on the weather." Whether a month begins is decided by the authority where you live; see The Hijri calendar.

Eclipses

  • List: the year's solar and lunar eclipses (for example "Total solar eclipse", "Penumbral lunar eclipse"), in date order, each with its date and magnitude, and whether it is seen from your place: "Seen from your place, start to end", partly seen, or "Not seen from your place". The next eclipse is open; tap any eclipse to see its contact times (Eclipse begins, Greatest eclipse, Eclipse ends, or the phases of a lunar eclipse) and what you see from your place. The arrows beside the title change the year. A year without eclipses says "No eclipses this year".
  • Map: choose an eclipse of the year from the buttons under the title to see it on the world map. For a solar eclipse, bands show how much of the Sun is hidden at most (under 20% up to 80% or more), with the Path of totality or annularity and the point of Greatest eclipse. For a lunar eclipse, the map shows where The whole eclipse with the Moon up is seen, and where only Part of it, at moonrise or moonset.

Sky: the planets

The Planets page lists Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto, each with whether it can be seen now ("Visible now", "Up, but the sky is bright", "Below the horizon"), its magnitude and its constellation. Tap a planet to see its rise, culmination and set on the selected day, and its phase, apparent diameter, elongation, distances from the Earth and the Sun, light time, position in the sky and, for Saturn, the tilt of its rings. Tap it again to close it.

Geographic info: magnetism

The Magnetism page shows the Earth's magnetic field on a world map, from the World Magnetic Model (WMM2025). Choose Declination (the angle between true and magnetic north), Inclination (how steeply a needle dips) or Strength. Coloured zones and labelled lines show the values; under At your place are the values for your location.

The page warns where a compass is unreliable, near the magnetic poles. The model is valid from 2025 to 2029; Taqwim says so when the selected date is outside that range.

The sky sphere

On the home screen, tap Sky sphere for a 3-D view of the sky: the Earth in the middle, the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars at their real places, with the celestial equator, the ecliptic and your horizon.

  • Turn the view by dragging. My place, Sun, Moon and Start view turn it to those points. The view-direction button holds the view Facing true north, Above the north pole or Above the south pole; tap it again for the next one.
  • Run time: the play button runs the time; the speed button switches between 1 min/s, 1 h/s and 1 day/s. Change the time opens buttons to step by a year, month, day, hour, minute or second. Now returns to the present.
  • Find in the sky: jumps to what comes next (the next season, eclipse or new moon, the Sun or Moon entering a constellation, the next perihelion or aphelion), or turns to the Sun, the Moon, a season, a planet or a named star.
  • Tap a body to open its card with its details; Look at it turns to it, Close closes the card.
  • Layers: the grid of buttons under the sphere shows or hides each layer: Planets, Names, Coordinate grid, Celestial equator, Equator disc, Ecliptic, Ecliptic disc, Horizon disc, Meridian, Celestial poles, Ecliptic poles, Zenith line, Line of apsides, Analemma, Earth size, Observer, Stars, Constellations and Star names. Taqwim remembers your choice.

Live sky

Tap Live sky to see the sky from where you stand. "Hold the phone up to the sky: the screen shows what lies behind it." If the direction looks off, move the phone in a figure 8 to calibrate the compass. On a device without an orientation sensor, drag to look around.
